abstract:
Wearable augmentation robots expand human motor capabilities, but every added degree of freedom creates a new coordination problem for the biological body. Although previous studies have made substantial advances in robot sensing, control, and safety, they have largely overlooked how the users own movement changes: individuals adapt their body movements when they start using an augmentation robot, even when control does not require it, and this coordination pattern continues to change as they gain proficiency. Consequently, users may struggle to accommodate robot-related restructuring of their movements during prolonged use, potentially increasing the risk of user rejection or abandonment. Over five days of training, 26 participants performed tasks with a wearable robotic digit and a tool-use control task, allowing us to longitudinally characterise and compare body-wide movement patterns between the two. Performance improved similarly across tasks, but the underlying motor coordination trajectories diverged. During augmentation, biological finger and limb coordination departed progressively further from its initial structure than during tool use, and joints increasingly varied together in ways that kept task performance stable, indicating that a new, body-wide augmented motor pattern continued to develop across days. These findings demonstrate that the biological motor system is not a fixed substrate that can be simply augmented with artificial limbs, but rather its movement patterns continuously evolve as users learn to control an added effector. Characterising this evolving motor solution informs the design, training, and evaluation of augmentation systems, supporting the sustained integration of added effectors into the human motor system.

One-Sentence SummaryRobots that work with the body face a moving target, as collaborating with one teaches people entirely new ways to move.
